Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

I picked it up on Tuesday, and the left front corner had lifted about a quarter inch. The top was cloudy near the lamp, and there were two dark rings beside the brass pull. The drawers still moved, but the bottom one scraped when it was almost closed. Mrs. Bell said her father bought it in 1962 and that he kept his letters in the shallow top drawer. She asked me not to make it look new. She wanted it to keep the little marks that showed it had been used.

Section 1: Initial inspection. I photographed every side before taking off any hardware. The back panel has three old nail holes along the lower edge and one narrow split that runs from the center toward the right stile. I measured the case at 48 inches wide and 34 inches high. The top is just under 18 inches deep. I first wrote 14 inches—no, 16—for the depth because I had the tape hooked on the overhanging edge. I changed the note before putting the tape away. The veneer is walnut over a lighter wood, and the legs are solid walnut except for a small repair block on the rear left leg. Someone had stained that block darker than the rest, and the stain had rubbed off at the floor.

1. Condition notes. The top has a thin finish, not bare wood, and there is a pale oval where a plant pot sat. The right side is in better condition than the left, but has a line of small dents below the drawer rail. The brass pulls are all original, as far as I can tell. The upper two are a little duller than the lower pair. Inside the center drawer, someone penciled a name that looks like Edith and a date that might be 1968. I did not try to erase it. The lower drawer has a loose dust board, and the left runner is polished where the wood has been rubbing. The back feet are slightly uneven on the shop floor.

Before I started, I told Cal that I thought the sideboard only needed a quick clean and a little wax. He said, “Look at that split again before you call it quick.” He was right. The split has an old glue line, and the panel shifts when I press beside it. I loosened the back nails with a small tack puller and saved them in a paper envelope marked “back panel original nails.” I did not pull the panel completely out because the right corner is stable, and I did not want to widen the old split. I brushed out the dust and used a narrow spatula to lift a curled chip near the lower edge. The chip stayed attached at one end, so I left it in place.

For the cloudy area, I tested a small spot under the back overhang with mineral spirits on cotton. The cloth picked up grime but not much color. I waited until the test spot dried before deciding the finish was still there. The lamp rings look lighter at the edges and darker in the middle. I did not sand them. I used a clean cloth and a little paste wax on the test area, and the cloudiness softened but did not disappear. Cal said that was probably enough, and I said, “Yes, for now.” I want to show Mrs. Bell the test before doing the whole top. She had asked to see any change first.

Section 2: Repairs. I cleaned the drawer runners with a dry brush and wiped them with a barely damp cloth. After they dried, I rubbed paraffin lightly on the contact points. The bottom drawer then closed without scraping, but it still needs a firmer push at the last inch. I found a loose screw in the lower left pull and tightened it by hand. The screw turned freely at first, so I used a thin piece of hardwood in the hole and let it sit before putting the pull back on. I kept the original screw and did not replace it. The shallow drawer still has a slight rattle when I slide it out, and I have not worked out whether that is the drawer bottom or the small divider.

The rear leg repair block needs attention, but I am not planning to replace it. The block is sound, and the old stain line shows where the repair begins. I will clean the surface gently and mix a small amount of color to make the light patch less obvious without covering the difference completely. I wrote down “walnut brown with a little raw umber,” but I need to make a test on scrap first. I also found a tiny crack at the top of the block, and it may only be in the finish. If the crack opens when the case is moved, then I will ask Cal to look at the joint with me.

Mrs. Bell called while I was putting the hardware back and said her father used to leave a folded newspaper on the sideboard after breakfast. She laughed and said the paper made a pale rectangle that she could still see in the old photographs. I told her about the rings and the test under the overhang. She said not to chase every mark and asked me to keep the penciled name in the drawer. I said I would. She is bringing a photograph of the room on Monday so we can check the color against the old curtains. The sideboard stood near a window in the picture, and the walnut looks warmer than it does under the shop lights.

Next steps are: let the back panel settle overnight, check the bottom drawer runner again in daylight, and photograph the test patch beside the uncleaned part. I should also put the saved nails and the loose screw in the small labeled bag rather than leave them in the envelope on my bench. I am not taking the pulls to the metal cleaner because the darkening is even and it seems consistent with the rest of the piece. If the humidity rises before Monday, the panel could move again, and I may need to wait before closing the split fully. I have not decided whether the top needs another coat of wax.
